strengths: The method is simple and practically motivated: retaining frozen linear heads while sharing the feature extractor substantially reduces stored network parameters and allows an inexpensive adaptation of iterated Q-learning.

The experiments provide concrete positive evidence across online DQN and offline CQL, two network architectures, and settings with and without LayerNorm. Reported results include a 6% AUC improvement over target-based CNN DQN and a reduction of the offline target-free performance gap from 26% to 6%.

Evaluation uses five seeds per game, IQM aggregation, stratified bootstrap confidence intervals, and individual learning curves. Ablations over the number of heads and normalization help establish robustness within the tested Atari settings.
The paper clearly describes the main algorithm and includes useful exploratory diagnostics of gradient similarity and feature rank.
weaknesses: The central resource-efficiency claims are incompletely evaluated. Parameter counts establish reduced network storage, but the paper reports neither peak training VRAM nor wall-clock measurements supporting its claim of comparable training time. Optimizer states, activations, and replay storage can substantially change the practical savings. No experiment demonstrates that the saved memory enables a larger, better-performing online network under a fixed memory budget.

The contribution builds closely on existing iterated Q-learning, but there is no direct comparison with the original i-QN to quantify the performance/resource tradeoff introduced by feature sharing. The shared ensemble control appears only offline, lacks a clear separation from iS-CQL within the reported uncertainty, and matches total heads rather than trainable heads. Online controls are needed to separate Bellman chaining from multiple-head representation learning and changes in exploration.

The explanation in terms of consecutive Bellman iterations remains heuristic. The shared feature extractor changes even the output of the frozen first head, and updates to any head affect the representations used by all targets. Gradient alignment measured along an iS-DQN trajectory and increased feature rank do not establish stability or identify the cause of improved performance. The causal language in Section 5.3 exceeds this evidence.

Evaluation is restricted to selected Atari subsets and DQN/CQL variants. Head count is varied and favorable configurations are highlighted, whereas baseline learning rates and target-update schedules remain fixed. This is a useful controlled comparison, but it leaves uncertainty about performance against comparably tuned baselines and generalization beyond these settings. Offline AUC over gradient steps measures optimization progress on a fixed dataset, rather than directly establishing improved sample efficiency.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the pseudocode and hyperparameter table: code release is promised, while LayerNorm placement, the precise multihead CQL objective and regularization coefficient, and treatment of optimizer states when heads are shifted are not specified. These details matter for independently reproducing the reported gains.

strengths: The shared-feature, frozen-target-head design is simple, clearly described, and practically motivated. It substantially reduces stored network parameters while retaining some benefits of target networks.

The empirical improvements are meaningful: the reported CNN-plus-LayerNorm result exceeds target-based DQN AUC by approximately 6%, and offline experiments reduce the target-free performance gap from 26% to 6%.
Evaluation includes two architectures, online and offline learning, head-count and normalization ablations, five seeds per game, bootstrap confidence intervals, and individual game curves.
weaknesses: The central resource-efficiency claims are insufficiently validated. Figures report parameter counts, but there are no measured peak training-memory results, wall-clock comparisons, or experiments reallocating saved memory to larger networks. Parameter savings do not directly establish training-memory savings because gradients, optimizer states, and activations also consume memory. The abstract's comparable-training-time claim is unsupported.

The contribution is an incremental adaptation of existing iterated Q-learning, without a direct comparison against the original i-QN method. Performance–memory–compute comparisons against i-QN and capacity-matched target-based networks are needed to establish the practical significance of the proposed compromise.

The experiments do not adequately isolate the benefit of the Bellman chain from generic multi-head representation learning or changed behavior policies. The shared ensemble comparison appears only offline, with overlapping aggregate confidence intervals. Online ensemble controls and an action-selection ablation would strengthen attribution.

The mechanistic conclusions exceed the evidence. Freezing the first head does not freeze its Q-function because shared features continue changing. Consequently, the fixed-anchor Bellman-iteration illustration is heuristic. Gradient cosine similarity measured along the proposed agent's trajectory and higher feature rank do not establish improved stability or explain the performance gains causally.

Evaluation remains limited to selected Atari subsets and DQN/CQL variants. The larger architecture uses a different game subset, weakening architecture-based explanations of head-count effects. Existing target-free methods are discussed but not directly benchmarked, and retaining standard hyperparameters does not establish competitiveness against appropriately tuned baselines.

Offline AUC against gradient steps measures optimization efficiency on a fixed dataset, rather than sample efficiency. Dataset-size experiments would be needed to support the broader sample-efficiency framing. Reproducibility is also incomplete: code is only promised, and important details such as the CQL regularization coefficient and exact LayerNorm placement are not specified.

strengths: The shared feature extractor with frozen target heads is a simple, practical design that substantially reduces stored network parameters. The algorithm and its relationship to iterated Q-learning are clearly explained.

The experiments provide concrete evidence of improved performance over target-free baselines: approximately 6% higher AUC than target-based DQN with CNN and LayerNorm, near recovery of target-based performance with IMPALA, and a reduction of the offline CQL gap from 26% to 6%.

Evaluation includes two architectures, online and offline learning, normalization ablations, and multiple head counts. Five seeds per game, IQM aggregation, bootstrap confidence intervals, and individual learning curves strengthen the empirical evidence.
weaknesses: The central resource-efficiency claims are incompletely evaluated. Parameter counts establish reduced model storage, but the paper reports neither measured peak training memory nor wall-clock training time despite claiming comparable training time. Optimizer states and activations affect actual memory savings. No experiment tests the motivating proposition that saved memory enables a larger, better-performing online network under a fixed memory budget.

The contribution is an incremental adaptation of existing iterated Q-learning, and comparisons do not sufficiently isolate the benefit of chaining Bellman updates. The shared-ensemble baseline appears only in offline experiments, where its confidence interval overlaps that of iS-CQL. Online comparisons with matched multihead ensembles and conventional i-QN would better distinguish chaining effects from auxiliary-head learning and changes in exploration.

The mechanistic conclusions exceed the evidence. Freezing the first head does not freeze its Q-function because the shared feature extractor keeps changing. Consequently, the fixed-anchor Bellman-iteration interpretation is approximate. Gradient cosine similarity and effective rank are useful diagnostics, but do not establish improved stability or a causal explanation for the return gains.

Generality remains limited to selected Atari subsets and DQN/CQL variants. The head count that works best varies with architecture and normalization, yet there is no held-out selection protocol or sensitivity analysis for the target-update period. The results support a useful improvement in these settings more strongly than a broadly established scaling method.

Reproducibility needs clarification. Code is promised rather than supplied; LayerNorm placement and the CQL regularization coefficient are not specified in the hyperparameter table. Section 5.2 describes the offline data using Agarwal et al. (2020), while Appendix A identifies Gulcehre et al. (2020), leaving the exact dataset provenance unclear.

strengths: The paper proposes a simple, useful architectural change: retain delayed linear heads while sharing the current feature extractor. This substantially reduces stored target parameters and integrates naturally with several value-based RL algorithms.

The evaluation spans online and offline Atari, seven difficult continuous-control tasks, and Wordle, using multiple architectures. Five or ten seeds, IQM aggregation, bootstrap intervals, and per-task learning curves provide substantial empirical support.

The improvements over matched target-free baselines are meaningful: the offline Atari AUC gap decreases from 26% to 6%, and the continuous-control experiments approximately recover target-based performance. Online Atari results also demonstrate benefits beyond merely retaining a frozen head.

Ablations examine head count, normalization, architecture, and an alternative shared ensemble. Target-churn and gradient-similarity measurements provide useful empirical insight, while runtime measurements show that the additional heads introduce little training overhead.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental relative to iterated Q-learning: the main advance is sharing the target feature extractor and retaining delayed heads. Direct comparisons with the original i-QN, including performance versus memory, are missing. The shared-ensemble comparison appears only in offline Atari, leaving the general advantage of the Bellman-chain construction incompletely established.

The resource-efficiency evidence primarily measures parameter storage rather than actual peak training memory. Optimizer states, gradients, activations, and replay storage can substantially reduce the practical percentage savings. Although the limitations acknowledge this, claims such as saving 33% of RAM in Wordle exceed what parameter counts alone establish. A fixed-memory comparison or measured peak VRAM would strengthen the central motivation.

Baseline hyperparameters are inherited from target-based implementations rather than tuned comparably for target-free learning. Sensitivity to learning rate and head-update frequency is not established. Appendix C's argument about Adam and loss scaling does not remove the need to check whether target-free baselines benefit from different optimization settings.

The benefit of multiple Bellman heads is setting-dependent. In continuous control, K=1 already recovers the performance gap, and K=9 adds no clear improvement despite an additional loss-discounting choice. Without LayerNorm, larger K can hurt. The conclusion that returns improve as head count increases therefore needs qualification.

The mechanistic evidence is correlational. Higher feature rank does not by itself establish greater useful representation capacity, and shared features mean that a frozen head does not define a fixed Q-function. The Bellman-iteration interpretation is a useful intuition, but the paper does not establish stability or approximation guarantees for this coupled update.

The Wordle AUC normalization needs clarification: returns are negative, so directly dividing their AUC by the target-based AUC would reverse the direction of improvement, unlike Figure 7. Any shift or alternative normalization should be specified. More broadly, a single small Wordle experiment provides limited evidence for scaling to language-model RL.

strengths: The paper offers a simple, useful architectural contribution: retaining a frozen output head while sharing the online feature extractor substantially reduces stored target-network parameters. Combining this with iterated Q-learning is straightforward to implement.

The empirical evidence spans online and offline Atari, seven difficult continuous-control tasks, and Wordle. Reported gains are meaningful: the offline Atari AUC gap decreases from 26% to 6%, and the continuous-control variant approximately recovers target-based performance.

Evaluation includes multiple seeds, IQM statistics, bootstrap confidence intervals, individual learning curves, and ablations over head count, architecture, and normalization. These provide concrete evidence beyond isolated favorable examples.

The target-churn and representation-rank analyses offer useful diagnostic evidence. Hyperparameter tables, runtime measurements, and the stated provision of supplementary code also support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The practical memory claim is insufficiently measured. Parameter counts establish savings in stored network weights, but do not establish equivalent reductions in peak training memory once optimizer states, gradients, activations, and replay storage are included. Figure 7's claim of 33% RAM savings is therefore stronger than the presented evidence.

Novelty is primarily an architectural adaptation of existing iterated Q-learning. A direct comparison with the original target-based i-QN, alongside memory-matched target-based models, would better establish the resulting performance–resource tradeoff.

The benefit of multiple Bellman heads is setting-dependent. K=1 already recovers continuous-control performance, and additional heads provide little benefit without LayerNorm on Atari. The ensemble control appears only in offline Atari, leaving the advantage of the ordered Bellman chain over generic multi-head representation learning incompletely isolated.

The mechanistic interpretation exceeds the diagnostics. Shared features make even the frozen-head target change during optimization, so the Bellman-iteration picture is approximate. Gradient similarity, target churn, and effective rank are correlational evidence rather than demonstrations that the proposed mechanism causes the performance gains.

The Wordle percentage improvement needs clarification: Figure 7 plots negative returns, whereas the stated AUC normalization divides by the target-based AUC. For negative AUCs, improved returns would produce a ratio below 100%, contrary to the reported direction, unless an additional transformation is used. The learning curves support improvement, but the percentage calculation is not reproducible from the description.

Generality remains bounded by selected Atari subsets and one small language-model task. Keeping baseline hyperparameters fixed gives a controlled architectural comparison, but does not establish superiority over comparably tuned target-free methods.

strengths: The paper offers a simple, useful architectural modification: retain frozen target heads while sharing the online feature extractor, then use multiple heads for iterated Bellman updates. It substantially reduces stored network parameters and is straightforward to incorporate into existing algorithms.

The empirical evaluation spans online and offline Atari, seven difficult continuous-control tasks, and Wordle, using several architectures. This breadth provides concrete evidence that the approach is useful beyond a single algorithm or domain.

The reported improvements are meaningful: CNN Atari with LayerNorm exceeds the target-based baseline by approximately 6% in AUC, offline CQL reduces the reported gap from 26% to 6%, and continuous control largely recovers target-based performance.

Multiple seeds, stratified bootstrap confidence intervals, individual task curves, normalization ablations, and head-count sweeps strengthen the evaluation. The gradient-similarity, target-churn, and effective-rank measurements provide useful diagnostic evidence.

The manuscript provides pseudocode, hyperparameter tables, and runtime/FLOP measurements, and states that code is included in supplementary material. These support reproducibility, although the supplementary code was not available for this review.
weaknesses: Novelty is primarily architectural and empirical, building closely on existing iterated Q-learning. A direct comparison against the original target-based i-QN is missing, leaving the performance–memory tradeoff against the closest predecessor incompletely characterized.

The central resource-efficiency evidence measures parameter storage rather than peak training memory. Optimizer states, activations, replay storage, and multi-head outputs can materially change practical savings. Although the limitation is acknowledged, measured GPU-memory usage and comparisons under a fixed memory budget would better support the deployment motivation.

The contribution of iterated Bellman updates is not consistently isolated from other multi-head effects. The ensemble control appears only in offline Atari, while online head sampling also changes exploration. In continuous control, K=9 does not improve over K=1 and requires an additional loss-discounting choice, limiting claims about the general benefit of iteration.

The mechanistic account remains suggestive rather than conclusive. Shared features make even the frozen-head targets nonstationary, so the Bellman-chain illustration is an approximation. Gradient similarity and effective rank do not establish that these properties cause the observed performance gains.

Some evaluation and reporting details constrain the conclusions: Atari uses selected subsets; language-model evidence consists of one small Wordle task; and baseline hyperparameters are largely inherited rather than comparably tuned. Appendix A also does not clearly explain how negative Wordle returns are transformed into the higher-is-better normalized AUC percentages in Figure 7.

strengths: The paper offers a simple, useful architectural modification: retain delayed linear heads while sharing the online feature extractor. Combining this with iterated Q-learning substantially reduces stored network parameters with minimal implementation complexity.

The empirical evidence is unusually broad, covering online and offline Atari, seven difficult continuous-control tasks, Wordle, and streaming RL. Reported gains include recovering the target-based baseline on normalized Atari and continuous control, and reducing the offline Atari performance gap from 26% to 6%.

The evaluation includes meaningful contemporary ingredients, including LayerNorm, BatchNorm, SimbaV2, and Stream Q(lambda). Multiple seeds, IQM aggregation, bootstrap confidence intervals, and individual task curves strengthen the evidence.

Ablations examine head count, normalization, target-update frequency, representation width, and mixed precision. The runtime analysis and explicit acknowledgment of remaining memory costs provide useful context.
weaknesses: The practical memory-efficiency claim is only partially demonstrated. Figures primarily measure parameter storage rather than peak training memory, which also includes gradients, optimizer states, activations, and replay. Statements such as saving 33% of RAM therefore overstate what is measured. There is no experiment showing improved performance or feasible model size under a fixed total-memory budget.

The incremental contribution over existing iterated Q-networks is not fully isolated. A direct comparison with target-based i-QN at matched head counts would quantify the performance cost of sharing target features. The shared-ensemble comparison is restricted to offline Atari, leaving unclear how much of the broader benefit requires the Bellman-chain structure.

The additional value of multiple Bellman updates is setting-dependent. In continuous control, K=1 already recovers the baseline and K=9 provides no clear improvement while introducing loss discounting by 0.25. Online Atari also changes behavior through random head selection, without a matched exploration ablation. These results support the frozen-head modification more uniformly than the proposed explanation for the multihead extension.

The mechanistic evidence remains correlational. Gradient alignment, target churn, and effective rank are informative diagnostics, but do not establish that these quantities cause the performance gains. Because the shared representation keeps changing, the frozen first head does not define a fixed Q-function; the Bellman-iteration illustrations should be interpreted as intuition rather than a convergence argument.

Some quantitative interpretations need clarification. AUC improvement is not directly a percentage reduction in samples required to reach a given performance. For Wordle, returns are negative, so the stated direct AUC-ratio normalization would reverse improvement direction unless an additional transformation is used; that transformation is not specified. The Wordle curves support improvement qualitatively, but the percentage claims are difficult to verify.

Generalization and tuning evidence remain limited despite the breadth of settings: Atari uses selected subsets, language evaluation consists of one constrained game with GPT-2 small, and target-update sensitivity is tested on only one game. Keeping baseline hyperparameters fixed while exploring several proposed-method configurations also leaves uncertainty about the gains over comparably tuned target-free baselines.

strengths: The paper offers a simple, useful architectural modification: retain delayed linear heads while sharing the online feature extractor. Combining this with iterated Q-learning substantially reduces stored critic parameters without requiring a second feature network.

The evaluation is unusually broad, covering online and offline Atari, seven difficult continuous-control tasks, Wordle, and streaming RL. Reported improvements are reasonably consistent across architectures and learning settings.

There is concrete evidence supporting the main empirical contribution: iS-DQN exceeds target-based DQN's AUC by approximately 6% with CNN and LayerNorm, iS-CQL reduces the reported deficit from 26% to 6%, and iS-SAC recovers much of the target-free performance loss.

The paper includes multiple seeds, stratified bootstrap intervals, individual learning curves, normalization controls, head-count ablations, runtime measurements, and detailed hyperparameters. These provide stronger support than a small proof-of-concept evaluation.
weaknesses: The novelty is incremental relative to iterated Q-networks: the main change is sharing features between online and target heads. A direct comparison with the original i-QN, including performance versus memory, would better establish the contribution beyond making an existing method cheaper.

Memory savings are established through parameter counts rather than measured peak training memory. Optimizer states, gradients, activations, and replay storage can substantially reduce the practical percentage savings. Although Section 6 acknowledges these costs, claims such as saving 33% of RAM in Wordle exceed the demonstrated reduction in parameter storage.

The experiments do not fully isolate the benefit of Bellman chaining from multiple-head representation learning and altered action selection. The shared-ensemble control appears only in offline CQL. Comparable controls in online settings would strengthen attribution, particularly because K=1 already recovers continuous-control performance and K=9 adds no clear benefit there.

Baseline hyperparameters are inherited from target-based methods, while the proposed method explores several head counts and introduces loss discounting for SAC. Adam's approximate invariance to uniform gradient scaling does not establish that target-free baselines need no learning-rate tuning. The target-period sensitivity experiment also covers only one game.

The Wordle AUC normalization needs clarification. Returns are negative, so directly dividing an improved, less-negative AUC by the negative baseline AUC should produce a value below 100%, whereas Figure 7 reports improvements above 100%. Any sign adjustment or transformation must be specified before the percentage gains can be interpreted.

The mechanistic conclusions are stronger than the diagnostics establish. Gradient cosine similarity, target churn, and effective feature rank provide useful correlations, but do not demonstrate causal explanations or guarantee stable learning of successive Bellman iterates with a changing shared representation. The language-model scaling evidence is also limited to a small GPT-2 model on Wordle.

strengths: The shared-feature target head is a simple, useful contribution: it substantially reduces stored network parameters while retaining much of the benefit of a separate target network. Combining it with iterated Q-learning requires relatively modest implementation changes.

The evaluation is unusually broad, covering online and offline Atari, seven difficult continuous-control tasks, Wordle, and streaming RL. Improvements over target-free counterparts recur across architectures and learning settings.

The reported gains are meaningful: CNN Atari performance exceeds target-based DQN by approximately 6% in AUC, the offline CQL deficit shrinks from 26% to 6%, and continuous-control performance approaches the target-based baseline.

The experiments include normalization-equipped baselines, multiple seeds, IQM statistics, bootstrap confidence intervals, individual learning curves, and runtime/FLOP comparisons. Hyperparameter tables and additional ablations provide useful reproducibility detail.

Target-churn, gradient-similarity, and representation-rank measurements offer informative diagnostics. Overall, the empirical breadth and consistent improvements place the paper marginally above the acceptance threshold.
weaknesses: The resource-efficiency evidence primarily measures parameter storage rather than peak training memory. Optimizer states, activations, replay buffers, and additional heads can materially affect actual savings. Statements such as 'saves 33% of RAM' are therefore stronger than the measurements establish; measured peak memory and comparisons under a fixed memory budget would better substantiate the practical motivation.

The contribution builds closely on existing iterated Q-learning, but experiments do not directly compare against the original target-based i-QN. The shared-feature ensemble control appears only in offline CQL. Broader matched-head controls would help separate the benefits of chained Bellman targets from auxiliary-head representation learning and altered exploration.

The Wordle percentage metric needs clarification. Figure 7 shows negative returns, yet better performance receives a normalized AUC above 100%. Direct division by the negative baseline AUC, as described in Appendix A, would reverse this ordering. Any shift or alternative normalization must be specified to make the reported percentage improvements reproducible.

Some reproducibility details are inconsistent: Section 5.2 describes the offline data using Agarwal et al. (2020), whereas Appendix A identifies RL Unplugged data from Gulcehre et al. (2020). The precise dataset and subsampling procedure should be reconciled.

The benefit of multiple Bellman heads is setting-dependent: K = 9 does not improve over K = 1 in continuous control and requires additional loss weighting. Target-update sensitivity is examined on only one game, and the extended head-count study uses two selected games. These experiments provide limited support for broad robustness claims.

The mechanistic explanation remains suggestive rather than conclusive. Shared features move even when the first head is frozen, so successive heads are not guaranteed to track consecutive Bellman iterates. Gradient similarity and feature rank do not establish causality or stability, and a higher feature rank alone does not demonstrate greater useful representational capacity.
